1:
Gill places this second muster after the exchange of the firstborn: the Levites having already been numbered once, they are counted again to pick out those fit for service. Calvin gives the reason in a line — that the charges might be equally distributed in proportion to the number of men available. Ellicott explains why the Kohathites come first though Kohath was Levi's second son: Moses and Aaron belonged to that family, and it was their office to bear the ark. Keil and Delitzsch describe the procedure as raising them out of the sum total of the Levites, numbered first and separately.

The age limits draw the fullest comment, and everyone starts from the contrast with the other tribes. Where Israel generally was mustered for war from twenty, the Levites were taken only from thirty; Ellicott adds that the earlier Levite census had counted them from a month old, this one being aimed at duties requiring considerable physical strength. Wesley makes thirty the age of full bodily strength and of maturity of judgment together, both wanted for work laborious and holy at once, and notes that John and Christ alike entered their ministry at that age.

Calvin argues the same limit from what youth is likely to do rather than from what age can bear. Vigour is needed for spiritual warfare, but so are seriousness and gravity; had young men been admitted, their levity might have detracted from the reverence due to sacred things, since the young are often carried into intemperate conduct by their own fervour. Access to the sanctuary was therefore withheld until they had grown into men, by which time it would be base to give way to the wantonness of youth. The upper limit he explains by the opposite defect, sloth being the common companion of old age; and he marks a difference from soldiering, since many are still vigorous past fifty — the stricter rule holding here because religion is more precious than any earthly business.

Henry reaches the same limits by way of the ministry now. Serving God requires the best of our strength and the prime of our time, and a man may make a good soldier much sooner than a good minister; before thirty he is in danger of retaining something childish and wanting the gravity the office needs. Henry lays the differing ages side by side — entered as probationers at twenty-five, and in David's time at twenty, when there was more work to do — and reads the gap as apprenticeship. He denies that the letter binds gospel ministers, taking two rules from it instead: that ministers must not be novices, unfit while still babes in knowledge for a work requiring ripeness of judgment; and that they must learn before they teach and serve before they rule. Release at fifty he calls a double kindness — to the men, that they might not be over-toiled when strength began to fail, and to the work, that it might not be done heavily by the infirm. His application is sharp: those who put off repentance to old age leave the best work to the worst time.

Clarke treats the discrepancy as a problem to be solved rather than a rule to be applied, setting thirty here against twenty-five elsewhere and twenty in Chronicles, and begins his reconciliation from the circumstances — the Levitical service at this period was exceedingly severe, and required men full grown. Henry and Calvin both notice what the text calls the work: entering into the host, or warfare. Henry will not let the military word pass. The ministry is a good work and a good warfare both, so that men ordained to it are ordained not to the honour only but to the labour, and must approve themselves good soldiers.
4:
Calvin asks why offices are assigned at all, and answers from what men do when left to arrange work among themselves. Promiscuous sedulity begets confusion, ambition stimulates some to put themselves forward, and disputes follow; unless a rule is prescribed men run about in an aimless hurry. God therefore comes forward and by his own authority confines them within their proper bounds. That the more honourable office falls to the Kohathites proceeds from his gratuitous favour, so that no man may boast of his dexterity or industry; and any envy the others might feel is removed once they hear how perilous the duty is, since death is threatened to whoever touches a forbidden thing.

What that charge amounts to is narrower than it sounds. Calvin insists the Kohathites were not to handle any part of the sanctuary, only to carry its vessels on the march after the priests had packed them; the priests being warned in turn that anything left uncovered would be the cause of their brethren's destruction. Two effects follow: reverence for holy things was increased, and the other tribes, seeing even Levites forbidden to touch the sanctuary, were reminded of their own unworthiness. Henry says the same of the covering. The holy things were veiled not only for security and respect but to keep them from being seen, which marked both the reverence due them and the darkness of a dispensation whose types were still unopened — whereas now, through Christ, the case is altered and we are encouraged to come boldly to the throne of grace.

Who does the packing raises a difficulty, since ordinarily the high priest alone entered the most holy place, and that on one day in the year. Wesley allows the exception: on this necessary occasion the inferior priests are permitted in. Ellicott suggests why it was no violation — at the moving of the camp the Divine Presence seems to have departed from the Holy of Holies and ascended in the cloud that gave the signal for removal. Both correct the name of the veil: not a covering thrown over the ark but, Ellicott says, the vail of the hanging, the curtain dividing the two chambers — Wesley's second veil, under which the ark stood while the tabernacle was pitched. Wesley adds the reason for the wrapping — the Levites who carried the ark might neither see it nor immediately touch it.

Gill is careful about the outer skins. They are not the covering that lay over the tabernacle, which belonged to the Gershonites, but one made on purpose for this use, to preserve the ark from rain and dust — Wesley says from the injuries of the weather — laid over the other coverings, so preserving the veil as well. Ellicott notes the staves were withdrawn while the covering went on, though at all other times they stayed in their rings. Keil and Delitzsch set out the order for the table: a hyacinth cloth spread first, the plates, bowls and pitchers laid on it, the bread laid on those, then a crimson cloth over vessels and bread together, then a sea-cow skin, and last the bearing poles put in. Gill gives the purpose — that these too might not be seen nor touched by the Levites — and notes that the scarlet went over the shewbread itself as well as the dishes.

Two terms want correcting. What is rendered covers to cover withal Ellicott takes for the cups of the drink-offering, and the continual bread he explains as bread renewed every sabbath and standing continually before the face of the Lord, this verse showing that it did so even during the marches through the desert. Wesley presses the difficulty: though the people had only manna for themselves, corn had to be reserved for the weekly baking of these loaves, procured, he supposes, from nations bordering the wilderness.
9:
Gill finds a scale of sanctity in the number of wrappings. The ark and the shewbread table had three coverings apiece; the candlestick has only two, the badgers' skins being here the outermost, because those other things were more sacred — and the ark, he adds, most of all. He notes of the lamps only that they were continually lighted and gave light in the holy place. Keil and Delitzsch list what went into the bundle with it: lamps, snuffers, extinguishers and all the oil-vessels used to prepare it for service, wrapped first in a hyacinth cloth and then in a sea-cow skin, and laid on the carriage. Ellicott corrects the word for that carriage — not a bar but a pole, or a frame made for bearing, the same term rendered a staff in the account of the spies.

The altar of incense is handled next. Gill explains the name: it is called the golden altar because it was overlaid with gold. Ellicott adjusts the preposition — they shall put in the staves, as in the earlier verses and again in the later one, not put to them. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same operation, the altar wrapped up with its own vessels, its bearing poles adjusted, and the whole laid upon the frame.

Wesley stops at the instruments of ministry, which he takes for the sacred garments the priests wore, and uses them to gather up the purpose of all the coverings under three heads. First safety, that these holy things might not be filled by rain or tarnished by the sun. Then decency, most of them having a cloth of blue or purple or scarlet over them, the ark wholly of blue — which Wesley ventures may be an emblem of the azure skies spread between us and the Majesty on high. Last concealment, which he calls a fit sign of the darkness of that dispensation: the holy things were then covered, but Christ has now destroyed the face of the covering.

With the brazen altar the scene shifts outdoors, and Gill marks the move — the holy of holies and the holy place having been cleared, they come forth into the court where the altar of burnt offering stood. Sacrifices being burnt on it daily there were always ashes to remove, especially necessary now, when the whole tabernacle was coming down. Keil and Delitzsch give the sequence: the ashes cleared first, then a crimson cloth spread over the altar, then all its furniture laid on top, then a sea-cow skin over the whole. Ellicott recalls that the pans for taking away those ashes had been ordered along with the rest of the brazen vessels, and corrects one item in the list — the censers are better called the fire-pans.

One vessel is missing from the inventory. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the copper laver is nowhere mentioned, probably because it was carried without any cover at all, and dismiss the statement supplied in the Septuagint and the Samaritan text about its covering and conveyance on a frame as a spurious interpolation. What is not mentioned but must have been provided for is the fire. Gill argues it was doubtless preserved and carried along with the altar or in a separate vessel, and reports Bishop Patrick's guess that it might have been carried upon the grate. Wesley makes the same inference: that the ashes only are ordered away implies the fire was kept, and since it had come down from heaven and was by God's command to be continually fed, it must have gone into some vessel, fastened to the altar within this covering or carried by a person appointed to it. He draws one further conclusion from the ashes — that Israel did offer sacrifices in the wilderness at other times, though not so constantly and diligently as they afterwards did in Canaan.
15:
Gill will not let the word sanctuary stand loosely. What Aaron and his sons had made an end of covering was not the holy place, nor the most holy place, since neither of those was covered by them, but the holy things within them — the ark, the shewbread table and the rest, which the Greek version reads so, together with all that appertained to them. Jarchi, he notes, takes the holiness here to mean the ark and the altar.

Ellicott returns to the vessel left out of the list and decides against emending the text. The Greek and Samaritan copies supply a clause about the brazen laver — that they shall take a purple cloth and cover the laver and its base, put it into a blue cover of skin, and set it on bars — but he finds no sufficient ground for supposing the Hebrew defective here, and thinks it more probable that the laver was simply not covered during its transport. On the verb that follows he prefers to bear, or to carry, without an object supplied, taking it of the whole body of the vessels of ministry already enumerated; and he observes that the passage draws the line sharply between what the priests do in dismantling the tabernacle and what the Levites do in moving it.

How the burden was carried and by whom afterwards Wesley supplies from the later history: on their shoulders, and in time the priests themselves, once they had multiplied, took these things up, though the Levites were not on that account excluded. The prohibition he reads narrowly and exactly — they were not to touch the holy things before those were covered.

Ellicott presses the same prohibition harder. The word rendered any holy thing may here, as elsewhere, denote the sanctuary itself; the injunction is repeated later in the book; and its enforcement is on record. Uzzah, most probably a Levite and of the family of Kohath, ought to have been acquainted with the law about removing the ark, and the outcome when he laid his hand on it shows what the threat meant. Ellicott adds the observation that gives the warning its point: the Kohathites, being the immediate assistants of the priests in respect of the vessels of the sanctuary, were of all men the most exposed to the risk of breaking this law.

The oversight committed to Eleazar is described twice over with a difference. Keil and Delitzsch make it a supervisory charge belonging to him as head of all the Levites — the oil for the candlestick, the incense, the continual meat-offering and the anointing oil, together with the dwelling itself and all its holy things and furniture; and they infer from the way the Gershonite and Merarite charges are worded further down that the services of the Kohathites fell under his oversight as well. Wesley takes the first half of it more literally: Eleazar himself is to carry these things and not commit them to the sons of Kohath, the oversight meaning his care that everything named be carried by the right persons and in the manner prescribed.

Ellicott goes through the four items correcting the renderings. The oil for the light is oil for the candlestick; the sweet incense is the incense of spices; the daily meat offering is better the continual meat offering, that is, the morning and evening minchah; and the anointing oil is the oil of holy ointment with which the tent of meeting, the vessels of the sanctuary and the priests themselves were all to be anointed.
17:
That God speaks again, and to Moses and Aaron together, is part of the meaning. Gill calls it a very solemn and awful charge given about the affair of the Kohathites, this being a hazardous employment. Keil and Delitzsch explain the repetition as precaution: to prevent any calamity befalling the Levites as they carried the most holy things, the priests are pressed by God's own command to do what was already described at length — for if the Kohathites came to the holy things before Aaron and his sons had wrapped them and handed them over, they would die.

The idiom of cutting off is the crux, since on its face it charges the priests with their own brethren's destruction. Gill collects the softenings: the Targum of Jonathan has give no occasion, and Jarchi be not the cause of their cutting off, through negligence or inadvertency in the packing and delivering. Keil and Delitzsch take it the same way, glossing the imperative as take care that the Kohathites are not cut off through your mistake and negligence. Wesley states it as an appeal to God's justice rather than the priests' hands — do not by your neglect provoke God to cut them off for touching the holy things. Ellicott justifies the harsh phrasing on a principle of speech: Moses and Aaron might be said to do that which would be the result of their negligence, exactly as Paul writes to the Romans, destroy not him with thy meat for whom Christ died.

The word for tribe is odd here. Keil and Delitzsch observe that it is not used in its usual derived sense of a tribe but in the original literal one of a stock or stem; Ellicott says the same, that it is used in a very peculiar sense and denotes only one division within the tribe of Levi. Wesley finds significance in the appointing of every man to his service and his burden, the services and burdens being equally distributed among them.

The one clause everyone stops at is the strange word behind seeing the holy things covered. Keil and Delitzsch derive it from swallowing — like a swallow, a gulp — and take it as a proverbial expression for a single instant, on the analogy of Job and with parallels from the Arabic in Schultens; and cite as illustration the judgment recorded in Samuel on those who looked into the ark. Ellicott builds his translation on the same reading: they shall not go in to see the holy things for a moment. Clarke keeps the literal image and gets something different out of it — when they are swallowed down, showing the promptitude with which everything belonging to the holy of holies was put out of sight; and adds that without this deepest reverence the mysteries could not have been to Israel the representatives of heavenly realities.

What the prohibition covered is worked out most carefully by Ellicott. The Levites were not permitted to enter the holy place where the priests ministered, still less the Holy of Holies; and whether or not that rule was relaxed while the tabernacle came down, as the bar against the Holy of Holies must have been relaxed for the priests, in no case were the Levites allowed to look upon the ark until it was covered. Gill agrees on the practice — they were not to be present during the packing, and were not to come in until all was covered out of sight — and reads it as a figure of how the mysteries of grace lay hidden under the former dispensation, when even the Levites were not admitted to a sight of them. Keil and Delitzsch close by defending these four verses against Knobel, who took them for a later interpolation into the original text; the linguistic grounds offered for that assumption they find weak throughout.
21:
Gill picks up two things the wording omits. Aaron is not named in the new command, yet he was as much concerned in taking the sum of the Gershonites as of the Kohathites; and though Gershon was Levi's eldest son, his posterity were not on that account excused from the service of the tabernacle or the bearing of its parts in journeying. Keil and Delitzsch note that the section is introduced exactly as the Kohathite one was, the duties being set out in agreement with the brief notice given earlier in the book.

Henry frames the two remaining families by comparison. Their charge was not so honourable as the first, but it was necessary and to be done regularly. The Gershonites had all the drapery — curtains, hangings, coverings of skins — to take down when the cloud removed and the holy things were carried away, to pack and bring along, and to set up again wherever the cloud rested. Aaron and his sons allotted each man his own piece, so that every one might know his work and there should be no confusion. Henry is struck by how many were employed: a far smaller number would have sufficed to lift the burdens, but the tabernacle had to come down and go up with great expedition, and many hands make quick work when each knows his task. He notices too what the chapter passes over: these men had tents of their own to strike and carry, but no mention is made of them — the young under thirty and the old above fifty might serve for that — because God's house must be preferred before our own, and preposterous was the care of those who ceiled their own houses while God's house lay waste.

Calvin looks at the same work and calls it what it is. The tasks enjoined on Gershon and Merari are apparently mean and laborious; it was hard and even servile labour to carry curtains and coverings, boards and bars and pillars. But hence, he says, we learn that in God's service nothing is to be despised, and that every part of our duty should be cheerfully performed, since it ought abundantly to satisfy us that God has deigned to choose us as ministers of his sanctuary — so that neither weariness nor pride should ever hinder us. Gill divides the two words of their commission on Aben Ezra's lines: to serve covers setting up the tabernacle, preparing the bread, slaying the sacrifices and keeping watch over the place, while for burdens covers what they did when the camp was journeying.

What exactly the Gershonites carried is where they diverge. Ellicott distinguishes the dwelling from the tent that covered it, and holds that the curtains of the dwelling constitute the dwelling itself, the woodwork being apparently regarded as subsidiary to them; those curtains were of fine twined linen, while the tent's were of goats' hair. Gill agrees that the first item is the ten curtains of fine linen. Wesley reverses the pairing: he takes the first word for the covering of goats' hair and the second for the ten curtains that covered the boards — the boards themselves, he adds, being carried by the Merarites. Both agree on the third item, which Ellicott identifies as the covering of rams' skins, distinct from the outer covering of badgers' skins, and which Wesley places next above the ten curtains. Ellicott would render two of the phrases differently again: the tent of meeting rather than the tabernacle of the congregation, and the hanging for the entrance rather than for the door.

The court is quickly settled. Its hangings, Ellicott says, enclosed the whole of it, and Wesley notes that the court so compassed both the tabernacle and the altar. Gill reads the clause about Aaron and his sons as meaning simply whatever those two should order and appoint.
28:
A second supervisor is named at the close of the Gershonite charge, and the commentators explain both the office and the man. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the charge being in Ithamar's hand as its being carried out under his superintendence; Wesley puts it as being under his conduct and direction. Ellicott adds the reason it fell to him. Ithamar had been actively concerned in the construction of the tabernacle, and as the special duties of Eleazar the elder son were assigned earlier, so now are those of the younger — the oversight of the Gershonites here, and of the Merarites at the end of the section.

Gill introduces the last family with a bare genealogical note: Merari was the third and youngest son of Levi. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the command about them runs in the same form as the command about the Gershonites, the verb used for mustering them being equivalent to the phrase for taking the sum.

The age at which a Levite began is not the same in every copy, and Gill records the variation without concealing it. The Greek version reads from twenty-five years old and upward, both here and in the parallel place, which agrees with the rule given later in the book; and he reconciles the two by making twenty-five the age at which the Levites went into the tabernacle to wait and to learn their business, while thirty remained the age at which they entered upon it.

What the Merarites carried is the plainest part of their commission and the heaviest. Ellicott says outright that theirs were the more cumbersome parts of the tabernacle and of the court, and thinks it probably on that account that in their case the specific duties of each man were assigned by name. Keil and Delitzsch parse the phrase for their charge as meaning their carrying, that is, the things it was their business to bear; and they explain the sweeping clause about all their instruments as covering everything used for setting up, fastening or undoing the beams and bolts. Ellicott corrects the verb at the end: not so much ye shall reckon as ye shall assign or appoint.

Wesley takes the same clause the other way and makes an inventory of it — every part and parcel was to be entered in a list. He asks why such a reckoning by name is required here and not in the foregoing particulars, and gives three reasons. These things were much more numerous than the others; being meaner things, they might otherwise have been neglected; and the requirement teaches us that God esteems nothing small in his service, and that he expects his will to be observed in the minutest circumstances.

The section closes as the Gershonite one did, with Ithamar named again over the whole of it, and Gill identifies the families involved by their old names, the Mahlites and the Mushites, as the ones whose service has just been detailed.
34:
Henry reads the three totals against the earlier ones and finds a lesson in the ratios. The Kohathites numbered 8,600 from a month old and upwards, of whom only 2,750 were serviceable, not a third part; the Gershonites 7,500, of whom 2,630, little more than a third. Of the many who add to the numbers of the church, he concludes, comparatively few contribute to the service of it; many have a place in the tabernacle who do but little of its work.

The third family reverses the proportion: the Merarites were only 6,200 in all and yet had 3,200 fit men, more than half; the greatest burden lay on them, and God so ordered it that though fewest in number they should have the most able men — for whatever service God calls men to he will furnish them for, giving strength in proportion to the work and grace sufficient.

Set against the fighting men the muster looks small, and Henry says so. The able men of Levi who entered into God's host to war his warfare were but 8,580, where the least of the other tribes had almost four times as many and some more than eight times; for those engaged in the service of this world, warring after the flesh, are many more than those devoted to God who fight the good fight of faith. Clarke is struck the other way. Laying the two censuses side by side, he exclaims at the number — so many men, all properly ecclesiastics, all performing some service by which God was glorified and the congregation benefited.

The arithmetic of the tribe is not agreed. Clarke's table gives 22,300 Levites in all, of whom 13,720 were unfit, being either too old or too young; Keil and Delitzsch put the total of males from a month old at 22,000, and remark that the 8,580 fit for service bears a just proportion to it.

What the work weighed Clarke alone tries to reckon: not less than about ten tons and fourteen hundred pounds of metal employed in the tabernacle, besides the immense weight of skins, hangings, cords, boards and posts; so that moving this temple was no easy matter, and the labour laid on the Levites while the journeyings lasted was severe. He then lifts the structure into type: tabernacle and temple alike represented the Church of the living God and the humanity of our blessed Lord, for as God dwelt in them so his fullness dwelt in the man Christ Jesus, and they were types in turn of the Christian Church, which is called the body of Christ.

Clarke then borrows a note from Ainsworth making the tabernacle an emblem of the body of man, working the parallel through four stages. As the holy things were first covered and taken away, so the soul is first withdrawn from the body by death; as the curtains were taken off and folded up, so the skin and flesh are pulled off and consumed; as the boards were disjointed, so shall our bones and sinews be; and as the dissolved tabernacle was set up again, so shall our bodies be at the resurrection. He grounds it in Paul's earthly house of this tabernacle and Peter's calling his death the putting off of his.

Calvin finds one more condition implied and one point established. None were to be received who were not free from defect and blemish — the blind and the lame had been excluded elsewhere lest their disfigurement produce contempt, and that they might be admonished by that sign to keep themselves the more diligently from all spiritual defilement. And because the inequality of the charges might have bred envy, God's authority is asserted at the close, where Moses records that he acted only ministerially and distributed the offices at God's command.
44:
Wesley pauses on the Merarite figure and calls the disparity providential. In the Kohathites and Gershonites, whose burdens were fewer and easier, only about a third of the whole number proved fit for service; in the Merarites, whose burdens were both more numerous and heavier, above half were fit. Here, he says, appears the wisdom of Divine Providence, which gave the strength where the weight was to be borne, and did not leave the heaviest charge to the family least able to bear it.

Ellicott stops at the grand total and does the same kind of sum. The 8,580 men between the ages named bear a just proportion, he says, to the 22,000 males of the tribe from a month old and upwards recorded in the earlier census: neither figure is arbitrary, and each stands as a check upon the other, the smaller number being just what a tribe of that size would be expected to yield between thirty and fifty.

The closing formula repeats two phrases that had been used a verse earlier, and Gill devotes his last note to both. The first, which the earlier verse gives as the service of the ministry — or, more literally, a service of service — Jarchi refers to that part of the Levites' work which lay in singing the song with cymbals and harps, calling it a service performed towards another service. Gill thinks Chaskuni explains it better, of the taking down and the setting up of the tabernacle, a duty incumbent on all the Levites without distinction rather than on the singers only.

The second phrase, the service of the burden, Chaskuni restrains to the ark, the table, the candlestick and the altars, which the Kohathites carried upon their shoulders. Gill would extend it further, to whatever each man of the three families bore and carried when the camp was journeying — which keeps the phrase as wide as the chapter that has just been detailing those loads.

What Gill will not let go of is the exactness. Every man was numbered according to his own service and his own burden; the ages ran from thirty years old to fifty, as Jarchi observes, because that was the order given to Moses; and the whole muster was carried out by the hand of Moses, with Aaron and the chief men of the congregation assisting, precisely as the Lord had commanded — Moses attending to it punctually, as a faithful servant in the house of God.
